```{r}
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(scales)
library(viridis)
library(knitr)
library(ggrepel)
sf_use_s2(TRUE)
```

## The question

Where can a visitor find the best local food in New Orleans (Cajun/Creole, Seafood and Southern restaurants), and which part of the city is the best place to look for it?

I picked local food because that is what people actually come to New Orleans to eat. Steps 1 to 6 find the restaurants, pick the categories, join the reviews and choose how to cut the city into areas. Step 7 rates the restaurants two ways, once with every reviewer and once with only the regular reviewers, each compared with their own habits. The answer at the end is a top 10 and a map of where they are, plus the neighborhood I would send a visitor to.

## Step 1 and 2: import and filter

The import is in [`R/import.R`](R/import.R). It reads the two Yelp json files with `stream_in()`, keeps businesses in New Orleans, LA whose categories include "Restaurants", and saves the result as rds. The review file is 5 GB, so that one is read 20,000 lines at a time and only the rows for New Orleans restaurants are kept. The section "How I handled the large files" near the end has the details and the import code.

```{r}
restaurants <- readRDS("data/new_orleans/business_new_orleans.rds")
reviews <- readRDS("data/new_orleans/reviews_new_orleans_no_text.rds")

dim(restaurants)
dim(reviews)
```

`r comma(nrow(restaurants))` restaurants and `r comma(nrow(reviews))` reviews. Every restaurant has a latitude and longitude, which matters for the maps later.

## Step 3: pick the restaurant categories

The `categories` column is one string with commas in it, so first I split it into one row per restaurant and category.

```{r}
restaurant_categories <- restaurants |>
  select(business_id, categories) |>
  separate_rows(categories, sep = ",") |>
  mutate(category = str_to_lower(str_squish(categories))) |>
  select(business_id, category) |>
  distinct()

category_counts <- restaurant_categories |>
  count(category, sort = TRUE)

category_counts |>
  filter(category != "restaurants") |>
  slice_head(n = 20) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Category", "Restaurants"))
```

"Restaurants" is on every row because that is how I filtered, so I dropped it from the table. After that the biggest categories are things like food, nightlife and bars, which are not really cuisines. The first real cuisine is cajun/creole at number `r which(category_counts$category == "cajun/creole")`, and seafood and southern are not far behind.

### Why these three

Cajun/Creole, Seafood and Southern are the three categories that describe New Orleans food. Gumbo, po-boys, crawfish, red beans and rice, fried catfish all land in one or more of these. They also overlap a lot in real life: a Cajun place usually serves seafood, and a lot of seafood places call themselves Southern.

```{r}
selected_categories <- c("cajun/creole", "seafood", "southern")

category_counts |>
  filter(category %in% selected_categories) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Category", "Restaurants"))
```

### Do they actually appear together?

```{r}
selected_wide <- restaurant_categories |>
  filter(category %in% selected_categories) |>
  mutate(has = TRUE) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = category, values_from = has, values_fill = FALSE)

pair_counts <- tribble(
  ~pair, ~restaurants,
  "cajun/creole + seafood",  sum(selected_wide$`cajun/creole` & selected_wide$seafood),
  "cajun/creole + southern", sum(selected_wide$`cajun/creole` & selected_wide$southern),
  "seafood + southern",      sum(selected_wide$seafood & selected_wide$southern),
  "all three",               sum(selected_wide$`cajun/creole` & selected_wide$seafood & selected_wide$southern)
)

kable(pair_counts, col.names = c("Categories", "Restaurants with both"))

how_many <- selected_wide |>
  mutate(n_selected = `cajun/creole` + seafood + southern) |>
  count(n_selected)

kable(how_many, col.names = c("How many of the three", "Restaurants"))
```

`r pair_counts$restaurants[1]` restaurants are tagged both cajun/creole and seafood, so the overlap is real. `r how_many$n[how_many$n_selected == 2] + how_many$n[how_many$n_selected == 3]` restaurants have at least two of the three tags. That is the evidence the three belong in one group.

### Inclusion rule

A restaurant is in my group if it has **at least one** of the three categories. Requiring two would throw out most of the plain seafood places and plain Southern places, and those are exactly the kind of restaurant a visitor is looking for.

```{r}
selected_restaurants <- restaurants |>
  semi_join(selected_wide, by = "business_id")

n_selected <- nrow(selected_restaurants)
n_open <- sum(selected_restaurants$is_open == 1)
```

That gives `r comma(n_selected)` local food restaurants, `r n_open` of them still open according to Yelp. That is `r percent(n_selected / nrow(restaurants), accuracy = 1)` of all New Orleans restaurants in the dataset. I keep the closed ones for the counts and maps in this part, since the question for step 6 is where local food restaurants are, not where to eat tonight.

## Step 4: join the reviews

Filter the reviews down to the selected restaurants first, then join. No reason to carry the other `r comma(nrow(reviews))` reviews around.

```{r}
local_reviews <- reviews |>
  semi_join(selected_restaurants, by = "business_id") |>
  mutate(review_date = ymd_hms(date), review_year = year(review_date))

reviews_per_restaurant <- local_reviews |>
  count(business_id, name = "reviews_in_dataset")

selected_restaurants <- selected_restaurants |>
  left_join(reviews_per_restaurant, by = "business_id") |>
  mutate(reviews_in_dataset = replace_na(reviews_in_dataset, 0))

summary(selected_restaurants$reviews_in_dataset)
```

`r comma(nrow(local_reviews))` reviews from `r comma(n_distinct(local_reviews$user_id))` reviewers, from `r min(local_reviews$review_year)` to `r max(local_reviews$review_year)`. That is `r percent(nrow(local_reviews) / nrow(reviews), accuracy = 1)` of all the New Orleans restaurant reviews, for `r percent(n_selected / nrow(restaurants), accuracy = 1)` of the restaurants. Local food places get reviewed more than average.

One check: Yelp's own `review_count` column counts all reviews ever, while the dataset only includes a subset of them.

```{r}
review_check <- selected_restaurants |>
  summarise(
    yelp_review_count = sum(review_count),
    reviews_in_dataset = sum(reviews_in_dataset),
    ratio = reviews_in_dataset / yelp_review_count
  )

kable(review_check, digits = 2)
```

The two are close (ratio `r round(review_check$ratio, 2)`), so the review file and the business file were taken at about the same time. I use the dataset count from here on because those are the reviews I can actually look at.

## Step 5: check the city label against the real city boundary

Yelp's `city` column is typed in by whoever created the listing. The census has an official polygon for New Orleans. A spatial join tells me which restaurants labeled "New Orleans" are actually inside it. The boundary files were downloaded once with [`R/boundaries.R`](R/boundaries.R) and saved as rds.

```{r}
louisiana_places <- readRDS("data/boundaries/louisiana_places.rds") |> st_transform(4326)
new_orleans_boundary <- louisiana_places |> filter(place_name == "New Orleans")

restaurant_points <- selected_restaurants |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326, remove = FALSE)

restaurants_with_place <- restaurant_points |>
  st_join(louisiana_places, join = st_within, left = TRUE)

restaurants_with_place |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  count(city, place_name, sort = TRUE) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Yelp city", "Census place the point is in", "Restaurants"))
```

```{r}
n_inside <- sum(restaurants_with_place$place_name == "New Orleans", na.rm = TRUE)
n_outside <- n_selected - n_inside
```

```{r}
outside_places <- restaurants_with_place |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  filter(is.na(place_name) | place_name != "New Orleans") |>
  mutate(place_name = replace_na(place_name, "none")) |>
  count(place_name, sort = TRUE)

outside_named <- outside_places |> filter(place_name != "none")
n_no_place <- sum(outside_places$n[outside_places$place_name == "none"])
outside_text <- paste0(outside_named$place_name, " (", outside_named$n, ")", collapse = ", ")
```

`r n_inside` of the `r n_selected` are inside the official New Orleans boundary. The other `r n_outside` say "New Orleans" on Yelp but the pin lands in `r outside_text``r if (n_no_place > 0) paste0(", and ", n_no_place, " of them are in no census place at all, so an unincorporated part of the parish") else ""`. Those are suburbs that use a New Orleans mailing address, so the pin is probably right and the city label is just loose. They stay in the dataset, but for the geographic comparison I only count restaurants inside the city, since that is the question.

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Local food restaurants inside the New Orleans city boundary, colored by Yelp stars."
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = new_orleans_boundary, fill = "grey95", color = "grey35") +
  geom_sf(
    data = restaurants_with_place |> filter(place_name == "New Orleans"),
    aes(color = stars), alpha = 0.7, size = 1.6
  ) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(option = "C", limits = c(1, 5)) +
  labs(title = "Local food restaurants inside New Orleans", color = "Yelp\nstars") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Almost all the dots are packed into the bend of the river on the west side: the French Quarter and CBD, then a thinner line going uptown. The whole eastern half of the city, which is mostly New Orleans East and the wetlands, has a handful.

## Step 6: choose and defend a geographic area

The question is "which part of the city", so I need to cut the city into parts. There is no one right way to do that. I compared three:

- **ZIP codes (ZCTAs)**, from the census. People know their ZIP code, but ZIPs were drawn for mail routes and some cover several very different neighborhoods.
- **Census tracts**, also from the census. Drawn to hold a few thousand people each, so they are small and even, but they only have numbers for names.
- **Neighborhood Statistical Areas (NSAs)**, from the City of New Orleans open data site. Named neighborhoods like French Quarter, Marigny, Bywater, Garden District.

```{r}
zctas <- readRDS("data/boundaries/zctas_701.rds") |> st_transform(4326)
tracts <- readRDS("data/boundaries/orleans_tracts.rds") |> st_transform(4326)
neighborhoods <- readRDS("data/boundaries/neighborhoods.rds") |> st_transform(4326)

# the neighborhood file's name column
nsa_name_col <- intersect(c("gnocdc_lab", "GNOCDC_LAB", "neighborhood", "NEIGHBORHOOD", "name", "NAME"), names(neighborhoods))[1]
if (is.na(nsa_name_col)) nsa_name_col <- names(neighborhoods)[sapply(neighborhoods, is.character)][1]
neighborhoods <- neighborhoods |> rename(area_name = all_of(nsa_name_col))
# the file has the names in all caps
neighborhoods <- neighborhoods |> mutate(area_name = str_to_title(area_name))

# ZCTAs cover the suburbs too, keep only the ones that touch the city
zctas <- zctas |> filter(lengths(st_intersects(zctas, new_orleans_boundary)) > 0)

zctas <- zctas |> mutate(area_name = zcta) |> select(area_name)
tracts <- tracts |> mutate(area_name = paste("Tract", tract_name)) |> select(area_name)
neighborhoods <- neighborhoods |> select(area_name)

city_points <- restaurants_with_place |> filter(place_name == "New Orleans")
```

The same join for each system. For every restaurant inside the city, find which area it is in, then count by area.

```{r}
summarise_system <- function(points, areas, system_name) {
  joined <- points |>
    st_join(areas, join = st_within, left = TRUE) |>
    st_drop_geometry()

  per_area <- areas |>
    st_drop_geometry() |>
    left_join(
      joined |>
        filter(!is.na(area_name)) |>
        group_by(area_name) |>
        summarise(
          restaurants = n(),
          average_stars = mean(stars),
          reviews = sum(reviews_in_dataset),
          .groups = "drop"
        ),
      by = "area_name"
    ) |>
    mutate(restaurants = replace_na(restaurants, 0L), reviews = replace_na(reviews, 0L))

  tibble(
    system = system_name,
    areas = nrow(areas),
    restaurants_assigned = sum(!is.na(joined$area_name)),
    unmatched = sum(is.na(joined$area_name)),
    areas_with_none = sum(per_area$restaurants == 0),
    areas_with_5_or_more = sum(per_area$restaurants >= 5),
    smallest = min(per_area$restaurants),
    largest = max(per_area$restaurants),
    per_area = list(per_area)
  )
}

comparison <- bind_rows(
  summarise_system(city_points, zctas, "ZIP code (ZCTA)"),
  summarise_system(city_points, tracts, "Census tract"),
  summarise_system(city_points, neighborhoods, "Neighborhood (NSA)")
)

comparison |>
  select(-per_area) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Geographic system", "Areas", "Restaurants assigned", "Unmatched", "Areas with 0", "Areas with 5+", "Smallest", "Largest"))
```

```{r}
cmp <- comparison |> select(-per_area)
zip_row <- cmp |> filter(system == "ZIP code (ZCTA)")
tract_row <- cmp |> filter(system == "Census tract")
nsa_row <- cmp |> filter(system == "Neighborhood (NSA)")
```

### What the table says

ZIP codes: only `r zip_row$areas` areas, and the biggest one has `r zip_row$largest` restaurants. That is too coarse. Telling someone "go to 70130" is not useful, that ZIP covers the CBD, the Warehouse District and the Lower Garden District, which are different places to eat.

Census tracts: `r tract_row$areas` areas, so the opposite problem. `r tract_row$areas_with_none` tracts have no local food restaurant at all and only `r tract_row$areas_with_5_or_more` have five or more. Most of the comparisons would be between tracts with one or two restaurants, which is noise. And nobody knows what "Tract 133" is.

Neighborhoods: `r nsa_row$areas` areas, `r nsa_row$areas_with_5_or_more` of them with five or more restaurants, biggest one `r nsa_row$largest`. The names mean something to a visitor and to anyone from here. Unmatched points are `r nsa_row$unmatched`, so the boundaries cover the city fine.

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Number of local food restaurants per area, under the three geographic systems. Same color scale on all three."
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 5

count_maps <- bind_rows(
  zctas |> left_join(comparison$per_area[[1]], by = "area_name") |> mutate(system = "ZIP code (ZCTA)"),
  tracts |> left_join(comparison$per_area[[2]], by = "area_name") |> mutate(system = "Census tract"),
  neighborhoods |> left_join(comparison$per_area[[3]], by = "area_name") |> mutate(system = "Neighborhood (NSA)")
) |>
  mutate(
    restaurants = replace_na(restaurants, 0L),
    system = factor(system, levels = c("ZIP code (ZCTA)", "Census tract", "Neighborhood (NSA)"))
  )

bbox <- st_bbox(new_orleans_boundary)

ggplot(count_maps) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = restaurants), color = "white", linewidth = 0.15) +
  geom_sf(data = new_orleans_boundary, fill = NA, color = "grey20", linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(trans = "sqrt", option = "D") +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(bbox["xmin"], bbox["xmax"]), ylim = c(bbox["ymin"], bbox["ymax"])) +
  facet_wrap(~system, nrow = 1) +
  labs(title = "Where the local food restaurants are, three ways to cut the city", fill = "Restaurants") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank(), legend.position = "bottom", legend.key.width = unit(1.5, "cm"))
```

Same data, three pictures. The ZIP map is a few big blobs. The tract map is a mosaic where most pieces are empty. The neighborhood map shows the pattern at the scale people talk about: one bright strip along the river from the French Quarter through the CBD and into the Lower Garden District, fading out going uptown, and almost nothing east of the Industrial Canal.

### My choice: Neighborhood Statistical Areas

I am going with the neighborhoods for the main analysis. Reasons, in order:

1. They match the question. "Which part of the city" is a neighborhood question. A visitor asks "should I go to the Quarter or Uptown", not "should I go to tract 133 or tract 137".
2. The areas are the right size. `r nsa_row$areas_with_5_or_more` neighborhoods have at least five restaurants, which is enough to compare averages without one restaurant swinging the whole area. ZIPs are too few and tracts are too many.
3. The names are documented. The city publishes the boundaries and the names are the ones on neighborhood association signs and in local news.
4. Nothing falls through. `r nsa_row$unmatched` restaurants inside the city are unmatched.

What the choice hides: a neighborhood like Uptown or the CBD is still big enough that the best street inside it matters, and the map cannot show that. Also a few neighborhoods have one or two restaurants and their average rating will be unreliable. I flag those in the table below and will leave them out of the final ranking.

The requirement was at least 10 restaurants in at least 7 different areas. Under neighborhoods that is `r sum(comparison$per_area[[3]]$restaurants > 0)` areas with at least one restaurant and `r nsa_row$areas_with_5_or_more` with five or more, so it clears easily.

### Neighborhoods ranked by local food restaurants

```{r}
neighborhood_table <- comparison$per_area[[3]] |>
  filter(restaurants > 0) |>
  arrange(desc(restaurants)) |>
  mutate(average_stars = round(average_stars, 2))

neighborhood_table |>
  slice_head(n = 15) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Neighborhood", "Restaurants", "Average stars", "Reviews in dataset"))
```

```{r}
top_nb <- neighborhood_table |> slice_head(n = 3)
```

`r top_nb$area_name[1]` has the most local food restaurants (`r top_nb$restaurants[1]`), then `r top_nb$area_name[2]` (`r top_nb$restaurants[2]`) and `r top_nb$area_name[3]` (`r top_nb$restaurants[3]`). Count is not the same as quality though. The next map shows the average Yelp rating by neighborhood, only for neighborhoods with at least five restaurants so one place cannot drive the color.

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Average Yelp stars of local food restaurants by neighborhood. Grey neighborhoods have fewer than five restaurants."

rating_map <- neighborhoods |>
  left_join(comparison$per_area[[3]], by = "area_name") |>
  mutate(average_stars_shown = if_else(restaurants >= 5, average_stars, NA_real_))

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = rating_map, aes(fill = average_stars_shown), color = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_sf(data = new_orleans_boundary, fill = NA, color = "grey20", linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "C", na.value = "grey88", limits = c(3, 5)) +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(bbox["xmin"], bbox["xmax"]), ylim = c(bbox["ymin"], bbox["ymax"])) +
  labs(title = "Average rating of local food restaurants by neighborhood", fill = "Average\nstars") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank())
```

```{r}
best_rated <- neighborhood_table |>
  filter(restaurants >= 5) |>
  arrange(desc(average_stars)) |>
  slice_head(n = 5)

kable(best_rated, col.names = c("Neighborhood", "Restaurants", "Average stars", "Reviews in dataset"))
```

```{r}
fq_stars <- neighborhood_table$average_stars[neighborhood_table$area_name == "French Quarter"]
fq_rank <- which(arrange(filter(neighborhood_table, restaurants >= 5), desc(average_stars))$area_name == "French Quarter")
```

Among neighborhoods with at least five local food restaurants, `r best_rated$area_name[1]` has the highest average at `r best_rated$average_stars[1]` stars, with only `r best_rated$restaurants[1]` restaurants, so one new place could move it. `r best_rated$area_name[2]` (`r best_rated$restaurants[2]` restaurants) and `r best_rated$area_name[3]` (`r best_rated$restaurants[3]`) are right behind. The big purple block in the east is one huge neighborhood with just enough restaurants to get a color, which says more about how big the area is than about the food. The French Quarter, with the most restaurants by far, is only number `r fq_rank` of `r nsa_row$areas_with_5_or_more` at `r fq_stars` stars. Tourist areas get a lot of reviews but not the best ones.

These are plain Yelp averages. Step 7 redoes this with reviewer adjusted scores and checks whether the ranking holds.

## Step 7: ratings from all reviewers, then from regular reviewers

From here on the question is "where to eat", so I only rank restaurants that Yelp lists as open. The reviews of the closed ones still count for one thing: a reviewer's habits. If someone reviewed six local food places and two have since closed, all six reviews say something about how that person rates.

```{r}
open_restaurants <- selected_restaurants |> filter(is_open == 1)
```

### Plain averages, every reviewer counted the same

```{r}
all_reviewer_summary <- local_reviews |>
  group_by(business_id) |>
  summarise(
    number_of_reviews_all_reviewers = n(),
    average_stars_all_reviewers = mean(stars),
    median_stars_all_reviewers = median(stars),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

all_reviewer_summary |>
  semi_join(open_restaurants, by = "business_id") |>
  left_join(open_restaurants |> select(business_id, business_name), by = "business_id") |>
  filter(number_of_reviews_all_reviewers >= 20) |>
  arrange(desc(average_stars_all_reviewers)) |>
  slice_head(n = 10) |>
  select(business_name, number_of_reviews_all_reviewers, average_stars_all_reviewers) |>
  kable(digits = 2, col.names = c("Restaurant", "Reviews", "Average stars"))
```

This is what sorting Yelp by rating gives you, with a floor of 20 reviews so a 5.0 from three people does not top the list. Every reviewer counts the same here, whether they give five stars to everything or almost never do.

### Regular reviewers

A reviewer with one review tells me nothing about their habits. Following the project instructions, a reviewer is eligible when they have at least 5 reviews of local food restaurants (open or closed). This is how much that cutoff matters:

```{r}
reviewer_activity <- local_reviews |>
  count(user_id, name = "reviews_in_selected_categories")

threshold_table <- map_dfr(c(2, 3, 5, 10, 20), function(threshold) {
  eligible <- reviewer_activity |> filter(reviews_in_selected_categories >= threshold)
  tibble(
    minimum_reviews = threshold,
    eligible_reviewers = nrow(eligible),
    share_of_reviewers = nrow(eligible) / nrow(reviewer_activity),
    their_reviews = sum(eligible$reviews_in_selected_categories),
    share_of_reviews = sum(eligible$reviews_in_selected_categories) / nrow(local_reviews)
  )
})

threshold_table |>
  mutate(share_of_reviewers = percent(share_of_reviewers, accuracy = 0.1), share_of_reviews = percent(share_of_reviews, accuracy = 0.1)) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Minimum reviews", "Eligible reviewers", "Share of reviewers", "Their reviews", "Share of all reviews"), format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

```{r}
minimum_reviews_per_reviewer <- 5

eligible_reviewers <- reviewer_activity |>
  filter(reviews_in_selected_categories >= minimum_reviews_per_reviewer)

eligible_row <- threshold_table |> filter(minimum_reviews == minimum_reviews_per_reviewer)
```

Most people review one local food place and never come back. At a minimum of 5, `r comma(eligible_row$eligible_reviewers)` reviewers are eligible. That is only `r percent(eligible_row$share_of_reviewers, accuracy = 0.1)` of everyone who reviewed a local food restaurant, but they wrote `r percent(eligible_row$share_of_reviews, accuracy = 0.1)` of the reviews. Going to 10 would keep `r comma(threshold_table$eligible_reviewers[threshold_table$minimum_reviews == 10])` reviewers and `r percent(threshold_table$share_of_reviews[threshold_table$minimum_reviews == 10], accuracy = 0.1)` of the reviews, which starts to thin out the smaller restaurants. I stay with 5 and test 3 and 10 at the end of this step to see what moves.

### Each reviewer's own baseline

The fix for reviewers who rate everything high or everything low is to compare each rating with that reviewer's own average inside the group. A reviewer whose average is 5 and who gives a restaurant 5 has a normalized score of 0. If that reviewer gives a 4, the score is -1. A reviewer whose usual rating is 3 and who gives a 4 has a score of +1. The score is not a new Yelp rating. It only says whether the review was above or below what that person usually gives.

```{r}
reviewer_baselines <- local_reviews |>
  group_by(user_id) |>
  summarise(
    reviewer_mean = mean(stars),
    reviewer_median = median(stars),
    reviewer_review_count = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

category_reviews_adjusted <- local_reviews |>
  left_join(reviewer_baselines, by = "user_id") |>
  mutate(
    normalized_mean_score = stars - reviewer_mean,
    normalized_median_score = stars - reviewer_median
  )

eligible_adjusted_reviews <- category_reviews_adjusted |>
  semi_join(eligible_reviewers, by = "user_id")

baseline_check <- reviewer_baselines |>
  semi_join(eligible_reviewers, by = "user_id") |>
  summarise(
    reviewers = n(),
    average_of_reviewer_means = mean(reviewer_mean),
    whole_number_medians = mean(reviewer_median == round(reviewer_median)),
    correlation_mean_median = cor(reviewer_mean, reviewer_median)
  )

baseline_check |>
  mutate(whole_number_medians = percent(whole_number_medians, accuracy = 1)) |>
  kable(digits = 2, col.names = c("Eligible reviewers", "Average of their means", "Median is a whole number", "Correlation of mean and median"))
```

I use the **mean** baseline. With five to ten reviews per person the median is a whole number for `r percent(baseline_check$whole_number_medians, accuracy = 1)` of eligible reviewers, so a median based score can only land on a few values like -1, 0 and +1 and throws away most of the difference between a 4.2 reviewer and a 4.8 reviewer. The mean uses every rating. The two baselines correlate at `r round(baseline_check$correlation_mean_median, 2)`, and the restaurant level scores built from each are compared below.

### Raw versus reviewer adjusted, restaurant by restaurant

```{r}
restaurant_summary <- open_restaurants |>
  select(business_id, business_name) |>
  left_join(all_reviewer_summary, by = "business_id") |>
  left_join(
    eligible_adjusted_reviews |>
      group_by(business_id) |>
      summarise(
        number_of_reviews_eligible_reviewers = n(),
        average_stars_eligible_reviewers = mean(stars),
        average_normalized_score = mean(normalized_mean_score),
        median_normalized_score = median(normalized_mean_score),
        average_normalized_median_score = mean(normalized_median_score),
        .groups = "drop"
      ),
    by = "business_id"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    number_of_reviews_all_reviewers = replace_na(number_of_reviews_all_reviewers, 0L),
    number_of_reviews_eligible_reviewers = replace_na(number_of_reviews_eligible_reviewers, 0L)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(average_normalized_score))

ranked_restaurants <- restaurant_summary |>
  filter(number_of_reviews_eligible_reviewers >= 5) |>
  mutate(
    raw_rank = min_rank(desc(average_stars_all_reviewers)),
    adjusted_rank = min_rank(desc(average_normalized_score)),
    rank_change = raw_rank - adjusted_rank
  )

ranked_restaurants |>
  arrange(adjusted_rank) |>
  slice_head(n = 10) |>
  select(business_name, number_of_reviews_all_reviewers, average_stars_all_reviewers, number_of_reviews_eligible_reviewers, average_normalized_score, raw_rank) |>
  kable(digits = 2, col.names = c("Restaurant", "Reviews (all)", "Average stars (all)", "Reviews (regulars)", "Normalized score", "Rank by raw stars"))
```

```{r}
top_10_raw_ids <- ranked_restaurants |> filter(raw_rank <= 10) |> pull(business_id)
top_10_adjusted_ids <- ranked_restaurants |> filter(adjusted_rank <= 10) |> pull(business_id)
top_10_overlap <- length(intersect(top_10_raw_ids, top_10_adjusted_ids))
mean_median_correlation <- cor(ranked_restaurants$average_normalized_score, ranked_restaurants$average_normalized_median_score)
```

`r nrow(ranked_restaurants)` open local food restaurants have at least 5 reviews from regular reviewers, which is the cutoff in the project instructions. Within that set, only `r top_10_overlap` of the 10 best by plain average are also in the 10 best by normalized score. The mean based and median based restaurant scores agree with each other (correlation `r round(mean_median_correlation, 2)`), so the choice of baseline is not what drives this. What drives it is the small samples at the top: the first few rows above have 6 or 7 reviews from regulars, and one person rating a place 1.5 stars above their habit moves a 7 review average by 0.2. That is why the final top 10 at the end uses a higher floor.

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Each point is one open local food restaurant with at least 5 reviews from regular reviewers. Above the grey line, the regulars rated it better than they usually rate; below it, worse. Labels are the top 5 by normalized score and the biggest movers."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 6
movers <- ranked_restaurants |>
  filter(adjusted_rank <= 5 | abs(rank_change) >= 0.4 * nrow(ranked_restaurants))

ggplot(ranked_restaurants, aes(x = average_stars_all_reviewers, y = average_normalized_score)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey70") +
  geom_point(aes(size = number_of_reviews_all_reviewers), alpha = 0.6, color = "#2C7BB6") +
  geom_text_repel(data = movers, aes(label = business_name), size = 3, max.overlaps = 20) +
  labs(
    title = "Raw restaurant ratings compared with reviewer adjusted scores",
    x = "Average stars from all reviewers",
    y = "Average normalized score (regular reviewers)",
    size = "Reviews"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The biggest moves between the two rankings:

```{r}
ranked_restaurants |>
  arrange(desc(abs(rank_change))) |>
  slice_head(n = 10) |>
  select(business_name, number_of_reviews_all_reviewers, number_of_reviews_eligible_reviewers, average_stars_all_reviewers, average_normalized_score, raw_rank, adjusted_rank) |>
  kable(digits = 2, col.names = c("Restaurant", "Reviews (all)", "Reviews (regulars)", "Average stars", "Normalized score", "Raw rank", "Adjusted rank"))
```

```{r}
biggest_up <- ranked_restaurants |> filter(rank_change > 0) |> arrange(desc(rank_change)) |> slice_head(n = 1)
biggest_down <- ranked_restaurants |> filter(rank_change < 0) |> arrange(rank_change) |> slice_head(n = 1)
movers_small <- ranked_restaurants |> arrange(desc(abs(rank_change))) |> slice_head(n = 10) |> summarise(median_regulars = median(number_of_reviews_eligible_reviewers))

movement_by_size <- ranked_restaurants |>
  mutate(regular_reviews = cut(number_of_reviews_eligible_reviewers, breaks = c(4, 9, 19, 99, Inf), labels = c("5 to 9", "10 to 19", "20 to 99", "100 or more"))) |>
  group_by(regular_reviews) |>
  summarise(restaurants = n(), median_rank_change = median(abs(rank_change)), .groups = "drop")

movement_by_size |>
  kable(col.names = c("Reviews from regulars", "Restaurants", "Median rank change (either direction)"))
```

The ten biggest movers are nearly all small samples: the median number of reviews from regulars in that table is `r movers_small$median_regulars`. `r biggest_up$business_name` jumps from rank `r biggest_up$raw_rank` to `r biggest_up$adjusted_rank` on `r biggest_up$number_of_reviews_eligible_reviewers` regular reviews, and `r biggest_down$business_name` drops from `r biggest_down$raw_rank` to `r biggest_down$adjusted_rank` on `r biggest_down$number_of_reviews_eligible_reviewers`. With that few reviews one harsh or one generous regular decides the score, so I read those as noise rather than as something about the restaurant. The second table shows the pattern: the fewer regular reviews a place has, the further it moves. Restaurants with 100 or more regular reviews move a median of `r movement_by_size$median_rank_change[movement_by_size$regular_reviews == "100 or more"]` ranks out of `r nrow(ranked_restaurants)`, so for the well reviewed places the plain average and the adjusted score mostly agree.

### Neighborhoods, raw versus adjusted

The same comparison one level up. Each open restaurant gets its neighborhood from the step 6 join, and a neighborhood is ranked only when it has at least three restaurants with a normalized score, so one place cannot decide a whole neighborhood.

```{r}
open_neighborhoods <- city_points |>
  filter(is_open == 1) |>
  st_join(neighborhoods, join = st_within, left = TRUE) |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  select(business_id, area_name)

ranked_restaurants <- ranked_restaurants |>
  left_join(open_neighborhoods, by = "business_id")

neighborhood_comparison <- ranked_restaurants |>
  filter(!is.na(area_name)) |>
  group_by(area_name) |>
  summarise(
    restaurants_ranked = n(),
    reviews = sum(number_of_reviews_all_reviewers),
    average_stars_all_reviewers = mean(average_stars_all_reviewers),
    average_normalized_score = mean(average_normalized_score),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(restaurants_ranked >= 3) |>
  mutate(
    raw_rank = min_rank(desc(average_stars_all_reviewers)),
    adjusted_rank = min_rank(desc(average_normalized_score))
  ) |>
  arrange(adjusted_rank)

neighborhood_comparison |>
  kable(digits = 2, col.names = c("Neighborhood", "Restaurants ranked", "Reviews", "Average stars (all)", "Average normalized score", "Raw rank", "Adjusted rank"), format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-neighborhoods-adjusted
#| fig-cap: "Neighborhoods with at least three ranked local food restaurants. Point size is the number of ranked restaurants."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 6
ggplot(neighborhood_comparison, aes(x = average_stars_all_reviewers, y = average_normalized_score)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey70") +
  geom_point(aes(size = restaurants_ranked), alpha = 0.7, color = "#D55E00") +
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = area_name), size = 3.2, max.overlaps = 25) +
  labs(
    title = "Neighborhoods: plain Yelp average versus reviewer adjusted score",
    x = "Average stars from all reviewers",
    y = "Average normalized score",
    size = "Ranked\nrestaurants"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
nb <- function(name) neighborhood_comparison |> filter(area_name == name)
fq <- nb("French Quarter")
cbd <- nb("Central Business District")
uptown <- nb("Uptown")
central_city <- nb("Central City")
freret <- nb("Freret")
seventh <- nb("Seventh Ward")
n_nb <- nrow(neighborhood_comparison)
```

The French Quarter and the CBD, with `r fq$restaurants_ranked` and `r cbd$restaurants_ranked` ranked restaurants between them, sit near the bottom both ways: the French Quarter is `r fq$raw_rank` of `r n_nb` on plain stars and `r fq$adjusted_rank` of `r n_nb` after the adjustment, the CBD `r cbd$raw_rank` and `r cbd$adjusted_rank`. The adjustment does not move them up. What it changes is the top of the table. Freret, which led the plain average in step 6, falls from `r freret$raw_rank` to `r freret$adjusted_rank`, and Seventh Ward from `r seventh$raw_rank` to `r seventh$adjusted_rank`: their regulars gave them about what those regulars give everything. Uptown goes the other way, from `r uptown$raw_rank` to `r uptown$adjusted_rank`, and Central City from `r central_city$raw_rank` to `r central_city$adjusted_rank` with `r central_city$restaurants_ranked` ranked restaurants, which makes it the best of the neighborhoods that actually have a lot of choice.

### Does the threshold change the answer?

The whole ranking rebuilt with a minimum of 3, 5 and 10 reviews per reviewer. The final list in the next section keeps restaurants with at least 10 reviews from regulars that sit inside a neighborhood, so that is the set compared here.

```{r}
rank_under_threshold <- function(threshold) {
  eligible <- reviewer_activity |> filter(reviews_in_selected_categories >= threshold)

  category_reviews_adjusted |>
    semi_join(eligible, by = "user_id") |>
    group_by(business_id) |>
    summarise(regular_reviews = n(), normalized = mean(normalized_mean_score), .groups = "drop") |>
    inner_join(open_restaurants |> select(business_id, business_name), by = "business_id") |>
    left_join(open_neighborhoods, by = "business_id") |>
    filter(regular_reviews >= 10, !is.na(area_name)) |>
    arrange(desc(normalized), desc(regular_reviews))
}

main_top_10 <- rank_under_threshold(minimum_reviews_per_reviewer) |> slice_head(n = 10)

threshold_effect <- map_dfr(c(3, 5, 10), function(threshold) {
  ranking <- rank_under_threshold(threshold)
  top <- ranking |> slice_head(n = 10)
  by_area <- ranking |>
    group_by(area_name) |>
    summarise(n = n(), score = mean(normalized), .groups = "drop") |>
    filter(n >= 3) |>
    arrange(desc(score))

  tibble(
    minimum_reviews = threshold,
    restaurants_ranked = nrow(ranking),
    shared_with_main_top_10 = length(intersect(top$business_id, main_top_10$business_id)),
    central_city_rank = paste(which(by_area$area_name == "Central City"), "of", nrow(by_area)),
    french_quarter_rank = paste(which(by_area$area_name == "French Quarter"), "of", nrow(by_area))
  )
})

threshold_effect |>
  kable(col.names = c("Minimum reviews per reviewer", "Restaurants ranked", "Top 10 shared with the main list", "Central City rank", "French Quarter rank"))
```

```{r}
shared_3 <- threshold_effect$shared_with_main_top_10[threshold_effect$minimum_reviews == 3]
shared_10 <- threshold_effect$shared_with_main_top_10[threshold_effect$minimum_reviews == 10]
```

The exact top 10 is sensitive: with a minimum of 3 only `r shared_3` of the 10 names stay, with 10 only `r shared_10`. That is the small sample problem again. With 10 to 20 regular reviews per place, a few reviewers decide the order. The neighborhood picture moves less. The last two columns rank the neighborhoods with at least three ranked restaurants under each threshold (the numbers differ from the big table above because this set has the 10 review floor): Central City is `r paste(threshold_effect$central_city_rank, collapse = ", ")` and the French Quarter is `r paste(threshold_effect$french_quarter_rank, collapse = ", ")`. Central City stays in the top half every time and the French Quarter stays in the bottom third. So I trust the neighborhood conclusion more than any single position in the top 10, and say so in the answer.

## The answer

### Top 10 local food restaurants

The rule: open restaurants inside a New Orleans neighborhood, with at least 10 reviews from regular reviewers, ranked by the normalized score. I raised the floor from the project's 5 to 10 because at 5 the top of the list was places with 6 or 7 regular reviews, where one review moves the score by 0.2. Ten is still a small number, so the plain average and both review counts are next to each score.

```{r}
top_10 <- ranked_restaurants |>
  filter(!is.na(area_name), number_of_reviews_eligible_reviewers >= 10) |>
  arrange(desc(average_normalized_score), desc(number_of_reviews_eligible_reviewers)) |>
  slice_head(n = 10) |>
  mutate(rank = row_number())

top_10 |>
  select(rank, business_name, area_name, average_normalized_score, average_stars_all_reviewers, number_of_reviews_all_reviewers, number_of_reviews_eligible_reviewers) |>
  kable(digits = 2, col.names = c("Rank", "Restaurant", "Neighborhood", "Normalized score", "Average stars (all)", "Reviews (all)", "Reviews (regulars)"), format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-top10-map
#| fig-cap: "The top 10 local food restaurants by reviewer adjusted score, on the Neighborhood Statistical Area boundaries. Neighborhoods are shaded by how many open local food restaurants they have. The map is zoomed to the part of the city that holds all ten."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 8
open_counts <- open_neighborhoods |>
  filter(!is.na(area_name)) |>
  count(area_name, name = "open_local_food")

top_10_points <- top_10 |>
  left_join(open_restaurants |> select(business_id, longitude, latitude), by = "business_id") |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326, remove = FALSE)

zoom <- st_bbox(top_10_points)
pad <- 0.025

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = neighborhoods |> left_join(open_counts, by = "area_name"), aes(fill = open_local_food), color = "white", linewidth = 0.25) +
  geom_sf(data = new_orleans_boundary, fill = NA, color = "grey20", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_sf(data = top_10_points, shape = 21, fill = "#FFD700", color = "black", size = 3.5) +
  geom_label_repel(
    data = top_10_points,
    aes(label = paste0(rank, ". ", business_name), geometry = geometry),
    stat = "sf_coordinates",
    size = 3,
    min.segment.length = 0,
    max.overlaps = 20
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "D", na.value = "grey92", trans = "sqrt") +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(zoom["xmin"] - pad, zoom["xmax"] + pad), ylim = c(zoom["ymin"] - pad, zoom["ymax"] + pad)) +
  labs(
    title = "Top 10 local food restaurants in New Orleans",
    subtitle = "Reviewer adjusted score, open restaurants, at least 10 reviews from regular reviewers",
    fill = "Open local food\nrestaurants",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank())
```

```{r}
top_10_areas <- top_10 |> count(area_name, sort = TRUE)
fq_in_top <- sum(top_10$area_name == "French Quarter")
cbd_in_top <- sum(top_10$area_name == "Central Business District")
uptown_in_top <- sum(top_10$area_name == "Uptown")
big_neighborhoods <- neighborhood_comparison |> filter(restaurants_ranked > 10) |> arrange(adjusted_rank)
```

### Which part of the city

The French Quarter is not the place. It has the most local food restaurants in the city (`r neighborhood_table$restaurants[neighborhood_table$area_name == "French Quarter"]`), the most reviews by far, and `r if (fq_in_top == 0) "none" else fq_in_top` of the top 10. Its plain average is `r fq$raw_rank` of `r n_nb` neighborhoods and its adjusted score is `r fq$adjusted_rank` of `r n_nb`. The CBD next door is the same story, with `r cbd_in_top` of the top 10 (`r paste(top_10$business_name[top_10$area_name == "Central Business District"], collapse = ", ")`) and a rank of `r cbd$adjusted_rank` of `r n_nb`.

The ten best spread over `r nrow(top_10_areas)` neighborhoods, so there is no single block to point at. If I had to name one area it would be **`r big_neighborhoods$area_name[1]`**: it has `r big_neighborhoods$restaurants_ranked[1]` ranked local food restaurants, the top restaurant on the list (`r top_10$business_name[1]`, `r top_10$area_name[1]`) and the best adjusted score of the `r nrow(big_neighborhoods)` neighborhoods with more than ten ranked restaurants. **Uptown**, a short streetcar ride upriver, has the number `r uptown$adjusted_rank` adjusted score of all `r n_nb` neighborhoods and `r uptown_in_top` of the top 10. The Lower Garden District and Mid-City have plenty of local food restaurants too, but both sit further down the table once the regulars have their say. So my answer is Central City and Uptown, not the French Quarter.

## How I handled the large files

The Yelp download is one 4 GB file that unpacks to about 9 GB of json, so the first thing to check was free disk space, about 15 GB with the download and the unpacked files side by side. The download and the unzip went through without trouble on my laptop, which has 24 GB of RAM. The business file (120 MB) is not a problem; `stream_in()` reads it in one go. The review file is 5 GB with about 7 million rows. I did not try to read that whole. jsonlite builds the entire table in memory, and 7 million rows with the review text would take several times the file size; with 24 GB it might have fit, but the chunked read was the safer choice and costs a few lines of code. `R/import.R` reads the file 20,000 lines at a time: `stream_in()` parses a chunk, hands it to a small handler function, and the handler keeps only the rows whose `business_id` is a New Orleans restaurant. Only the kept rows ever sit in memory. The whole import, both files, took about 6 minutes.

What came out is small. The restaurant table is `r round(file.size("data/new_orleans/business_new_orleans.rds") / 1e6, 1)` MB and the review table without the text is `r round(file.size("data/new_orleans/reviews_new_orleans_no_text.rds") / 1e6, 1)` MB as xz compressed rds, so both are committed and everything in this report runs off them. The version with the review text is far bigger and stays on my computer, in `.gitignore` next to `data/raw/`. I kept the raw json files on the laptop too, in case the import had to be run again. Now that the rds files are committed they can be deleted.

```{r}
#| file: R/import.R
#| eval: false
```

## Limitations

- The dataset is the sample Yelp chose to release, not all of Yelp. The step 4 check showed the dataset holds about as many reviews as Yelp's own `review_count`, but every average here is an average of the reviews in the file.
- Reviews run from `r min(local_reviews$review_year)` to `r max(local_reviews$review_year)`. A restaurant can change hands in that time, and `is_open` is Yelp's status when the dataset was built, not today's.
- The reviewer baseline is computed inside the local food group only, as the project instructions describe. A regular who gives every local food place 5 stars gets a normalized score of 0 for all of them, which says more about having five reviews than about the food. The threshold tables show how many reviewers this touches and how much the ranking moves.
- The normalized score is a difference from a reviewer's habit, not a rating. Two restaurants with the same score can have very different star averages, which is why the plain average is always shown next to it.
- `r n_outside` restaurants with a New Orleans label sit outside the official boundary and `r sum(open_restaurants$is_open == 1) - sum(!is.na(open_neighborhoods$area_name))` open local food restaurants have no neighborhood, so they are counted but cannot be on the final map.
- A neighborhood average flattens the good block and the bad block inside it, and the neighborhoods with three to five ranked restaurants have averages that one place can move.

## Packages

```{r}
package_names <- c("tidyverse", "jsonlite", "lubridate", "sf", "tigris", "scales", "viridis", "ggrepel", "knitr")
package_versions <- map_chr(package_names, function(package) {
  if (requireNamespace(package, quietly = TRUE)) as.character(packageVersion(package)) else "not installed"
})
tibble(package = package_names, version = package_versions) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Package", "Version"))
```

`ggrepel` is the one package beyond the project's list. It keeps the labels on the maps from sitting on top of each other. `tigris` is only used by `R/boundaries.R`. R `r paste(R.version$major, R.version$minor, sep = ".")`.
